# Case study: a security team's alert triage {#sec-ch18}

::: {.epigraph by="Mike Tyson, attributed"}
Everybody has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.
:::

Each chapter so far took one piece of the problem: calibration, a threshold, an agent, a pattern. This one runs the whole thing start to finish, the way a real team would: the team as it was, the new system run quietly for a week before it may act, then switched on, and then a phishing campaign.

It doesn't all work perfectly. That's the point of a case study: where it helps a lot, where it helps less than you'd hope, and the one assumption that mattered most.

::: {.goals}
- Describe triage before a decision layer, and measure what it misses without anyone noticing.
- Build the system from the book's pieces, and name which chapter each piece comes from.
- Run a new decision system in shadow mode before it acts, and read what shadow mode shows.
- See why the order of a review queue matters as much as its size.
- Handle a campaign that changes the base rate, with monitoring, recalibration and overtime.
:::

## Before: the queue

The team gets about {{< num ch21 live_per_day int >}} alerts a day. Six people clear about forty each: a capacity of {{< num ch25 capacity int >}}. Before this project, alerts flagged by the senior expert's rules went to the front of one queue; everything else waited in arrival order; anything not reached within a day "aged out", closed unseen.

That's a very ordinary way to run things, and it hides its failures: nobody sees what ages out, so nobody knows how much of it was real. In our synthetic week we do know: about {{< num ch25 old.threats_unseen_per_day f1 >}} real threats a day were never seen by anyone.

![Where each day's alerts go, and where the real threats go, before and after. Before, most alerts aged out of the queue unseen, and so did a large share of real threats. After, most alerts are closed by the policy on purpose, and most real threats are queued or paged.](/figures/ch25/routes.pdf){#fig-routes}

The left half of @fig-routes looks similar before and after: most alerts get closed without a person either way. The right half shows the difference. Before, alerts were closed because time *ran out*, whether or not they mattered. After, they're closed by a *decision*, and the real threats mostly reach a person.

## The system

![The whole system, with the chapter each piece comes from. Alerts go to Jev as typed questions, the answers are calibrated, the policy routes each alert, and people see the queue and the pages. The LLM writes only for them. Everything is logged and monitored, and labels from reviews and a random audit feed back into calibration.](/figures/ch25/system.pdf){#fig-system}

There's nothing in @fig-system you haven't met. The alert's fields go to the decision model as three typed questions (Chapter 10). Platt scaling on three weeks of history calibrates the probabilities for this company (Chapters 3 and 11). The three-zone policy, with its thresholds set by cost and capacity, routes each alert (Chapter 14). The LLM writes the case note for the queue and the urgent message for the analyst on call, and nothing else (Chapters 15 and 17). And every decision is logged with its inputs, answers and policy version.

## A week in shadow mode

You don't switch a system like this on and hope. You run it in **shadow mode**: it sees every alert and records what it *would* have done, while people work as before. Nothing it decides has any effect.

::: {.keyidea}
Run a new decision system in shadow mode before you let it act.
:::

At the end of the shadow week, you put what it would have done next to what turned out to be true.

![Shadow mode's verdict, per day of the live week. Each cell counts alerts by what the system would have done and what they turned out to be. The red cell, outlined in black and striped, is the one to argue about: real threats it would have closed on its own.](/figures/ch25/shadow.pdf){#fig-shadow-18}

The meeting after a shadow week is mostly about one cell, the red one outlined in black in @fig-shadow-18. It shows about {{< num ch25 new_threats_closed_per_day f1 >}} real threats a day that the system would have auto-closed. That sounds bad, until you compare it with the old queue, which let {{< num ch25 old.threats_unseen_per_day f1 >}} a day age out.

It's also more than forecast: on history the same policy auto-closed about {{< num ch25 forecast_closed_hist f1 >}} a day. Say so plainly in the meeting: the forecast was in range but too hopeful, and the daily monitor will tell chance from trend.

The team switched it on with two conditions from Chapter 14: a random audit of 3% of auto-closed alerts, and a fail-safe that sends a case to review whenever a call fails.

## Order matters as much as size

One detail is easy to miss. The new queue is sorted by probability, likeliest first. In arrival order, with the same alerts in the same queue, the typical real threat would wait about {{< num ch25 fifo_wait int >}} minutes. Sorted, about {{< num ch25 prio_wait int >}}. Same people, same alerts, same queue. Only the order changed.

![How long it takes for a real threat to reach a person. Before, rule-flagged threats were seen quickly and the rest waited up to a day or were never seen. After, urgent calls reach someone in about fifteen minutes and the queue takes the likeliest threats first.](/figures/ch25/time-to-human.pdf){#fig-time-to-human}

The old way wasn't slow for everything: rule-flagged threats were seen within minutes (@fig-time-to-human). Its problem was the long flat tail, threats the rules missed, waiting behind everything else. After the change, {{< num ch25 new.threats_within_hour_share pct >}} of real threats reach a person within an hour, against {{< num ch25 old.threats_within_hour_share pct >}} before.

::: {.keyidea}
A probability decides *what* a person looks at first, not only *whether* they look.
:::

Ordering the queue is often the cheapest improvement available.

## The campaign

The system went live. Then a phishing campaign started: link alerts fired three times as often, and far more were real. @fig-campaign shows what it did to the team's work.

![The campaign week, day by day, with and without a response on day 3. Left: alerts sent to review, against the team's capacity. Right: real threats never seen by a person, added up over the week. Recalibrating link alerts and adding overtime helped, but it didn't make the problem go away.](/figures/ch25/campaign.pdf){#fig-campaign}

By day 1 the queue was over capacity (worst day: {{< num ch25 camp_peak_reviews int >}} against {{< num ch25 capacity int >}}). And link alerts' probabilities were now too *low*, calibrated on weeks when such alerts were mostly harmless. The daily monitoring caught both on day 2.

On day 3 the team responded: re-estimated the base rate for link alerts from what reviewers had confirmed, corrected those probabilities (Chapter 11), and approved overtime for two extra people.

It helped: real threats never seen by a person fell from about {{< num ch25 camp_missed_base int >}} to about {{< num ch25 camp_missed_resp int >}} over the week. But with honest probabilities, the queue grew *past* even the overtime capacity. Far more link alerts deserved a look than the bigger team could manage. The uncomfortable truth:

::: {.keyidea}
Calibration tells you truthfully how much work there is. It can't make the work smaller.
:::

When the world gets more dangerous, the decision layer's job is to show it early and spend limited time on the likeliest threats. The rest is how many people you have.

## After five weeks

![Triage before and after, on the same synthetic live week, with the same six analysts.](/figures/ch25/scorecard.pdf){#fig-scorecard-18}

@fig-scorecard-18 is the summary for the company's leaders. The team looked at about the same number of alerts a day; they weren't working harder. They looked at *different* alerts, in a different order, and more real threats reached them, sooner. (One row looks worse, the typical wait for threats that *were* seen, because before, those were mostly the rule-flagged ones at the front. The fair comparison is the row above: the share of all real threats seen within an hour more than doubled.)

::: {.breaks}
This is a simulation on synthetic alerts with made-up costs, capacities and response times; treat every number as an example of the method. Real teams differ: people aren't interchangeable, alerts arrive in bursts, other defences catch some threats later. Shadow mode is only as good as the labels you compare against, and the missing labels are exactly those nobody reviewed, which is why the random audit matters. And the campaign response needed two days of labels, so the system was wrong for two days first.
:::

::: {.threshold}
During the campaign, the company can pay overtime for two more analysts. Or it can tell the policy to auto-close more link alerts, to keep the queue at capacity. A missed threat costs about \$10,000; one analyst's day of overtime costs about \$600. The corrected probabilities say the extra reviews would find about one real threat for every six alerts. Which would you choose?

(Each extra analyst clears about 40 alerts a day. At one threat in six, that finds about 6 or 7 real threats, worth around \$65,000. That's about a hundred times the cost of the overtime. Add the people, and keep the thresholds where the costs put them. Making the queue shorter by closing likely threats just moves the cost to where nobody sees it.)
:::

The quality expert W. Edwards Deming used to say that a bad system will beat a good person every time. The team was never the problem. The old queue decided what they saw by accident; the new one decides on purpose.

1. What would the team need ready in advance to respond to the campaign on day 2 instead of day 3?
2. Write the one-page shadow-mode report you'd send to the head of security. What goes first?
:::
